unitDescription.value: In this unit, students design a website for a local business such as a café, shop, tradesperson or service. Students investigate how businesses use websites to share information, attract customers and promote their products or services. They consider the needs of different users and explore website layout, navigation, colours, images and accessibility. Students create user stories, develop design ideas and produce wireframes before building a functional website using GitHub Codespaces and generative AI. They test their website, collect feedback and make improvements to their final design. The unit focuses on user experience, design thinking, evaluation and the responsible use of AI, rather than advanced programming.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: In Digital Technologies, students should have frequent opportunities for authentic learning by making key connections with other learning areas.

description.value: Students design and develop an AI-assisted website for a local business. They identify the target audience, create user stories and design criteria, and investigate the information customers need from the website. Students develop a site map, alternative design ideas, wireframes and a simple visual style guide before using generative AI within GitHub Codespaces to build a functional website prototype. They test the website with users, collect feedback and make improvements to the layout, navigation, accessibility and content. The final submission includes the design work, working website prototype, testing evidence and an evaluation of the final solution.

conditions.value: 3–5 A3 pages or equivalent digital media pages; includes annotated user stories and wireframes, a functional website developed in GitHub Codespaces, and a 200–300 word evaluation of the solution against design criteria and user needs.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 8 students develop and modify creative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and evaluate alternative solutions against user stories and design criteria. Students acquire, interpret and model data with spreadsheets and represent data with integers and binary. They design and trace algorithms and implement them in a general-purpose programming language. Students select appropriate hardware for particular tasks, explain how data is transmitted and secured in networks, and identify cyber security threats. They select and use a range of digital tools efficiently and responsibly to create, locate and share content; and to plan, collaborate on and manage projects. Students manage their digital footprint.

moderation.value:
Internal moderation is conducted systematically to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Year 7–8 Digital Technologies achievement standard. This process includes:

*   **Standardisation:** Faculty review of the Guide to Making Judgements (GTMJ) and assessment parameters prior to the design phase to ensure a shared understanding of the evidence required for each performance level.
*   **Monitoring (Week 6):** Collaborative review of student wireframes and user stories to ensure consistency in formative feedback and alignment with design thinking requirements.
*   **Moderation Conferencing (Week 9):** Teachers meet to review student work samples at key grade boundaries (A, C, and E) to validate assessment decisions regarding user experience design and solution evaluation.
*   **Cross-marking:** Departmental cross-marking of a representative sample of final website projects to ensure the reliable and objective application of performance descriptors across the cohort.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students begin by investigating the significance of a digital presence for businesses within the Yeppoon and Capricorn Coast community. Through a series of comparative case studies, they explore how local entities, such as coastal cafés or regional tradespeople, utilise websites to communicate brand value and secure customer engagement. Lessons focus on identifying the distinct features of commercial sites, such as booking systems and service catalogues, contrasted against personal or social media-driven platforms.

resources.value: Projector for live site analysis, list of local Yeppoon business URLs, feature-comparison graphic organiser, digital design journal template.

theory.value: The theoretical focus is on the role of digital systems in supporting commercial objectives. Students learn to identify core website components including 'Call to Action' (CTA) elements, trust signals, and service-oriented information blocks. Explicit instruction covers how business goals—such as lead generation or information dissemination—influence the selection of digital features. Students examine the difference between static and interactive content and discuss how professional design contributes to business credibility in a competitive local market.

prac.value: Students conduct a competitive audit of three local business websites, using a structured criteria sheet to evaluate functionality and user engagement. They work in small groups to present a 'feature breakdown' of a successful Yeppoon-based site, highlighting specific elements that attract customers. Individually, students select a local business category (e.g., hospitality, retail, or trade) and define the primary purpose of their proposed digital solution, documenting their initial findings in a digital design journal.

assessment.value: Formative: Completion of the competitive audit table and the formal selection of a business focus with a justified purpose statement.

outlineTheme.value: Students investigate the role of digital presence for local businesses, such as Yeppoon-based cafés or tradespeople. They analyse how businesses use websites to communicate value and attract customers, identifying the key features that distinguish successful commercial sites from personal ones. Through case studies, students explore the relationship between business goals and digital functionality.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: This week focuses on user-centred design (UCD) and the process of defining functional requirements through the lens of the target audience. Students identify the diverse needs of potential customers and translate these into actionable design tasks. They use divergent thinking techniques to brainstorm features that solve specific user problems, ensuring the proposed website serves both the business owner and the end user.

resources.value: Persona development templates, user story sentence starters, mind-mapping software (e.g., Miro or Canva), design criteria guide.

theory.value: Students explore the concept of user stories and how they bridge the gap between user needs and technical specifications. The 'As a [user], I want to [action], so that [benefit]' framework is taught as a method for defining project scope. Lessons also cover the development of design criteria, focusing on measurable benchmarks such as mobile responsiveness, accessibility, and intuitive navigation. Students learn how these criteria act as a quality control mechanism throughout the development lifecycle.

prac.value: Students develop detailed personas representing various segments of the Yeppoon community, such as a tourist looking for opening hours or a local resident seeking a quote. They write a minimum of five user stories per persona to map out required website functionality. Using 'Crazy 8s' or mind-mapping techniques, students generate a range of design ideas to meet these requirements. The week concludes with students refining their ideas into a formal list of design criteria that will guide their final evaluation.

assessment.value: Formative: Peer review of user stories and a checklist of design criteria evaluated against the project description.

outlineTheme.value: Focusing on user-centred design, students identify target audiences and develop detailed user stories to define specific website requirements. They establish clear design criteria that address both business goals and the functional needs of potential customers, such as ease of navigation and clear contact information. Students practice using divergent techniques to brainstorm how these needs can be met digitally.

activities.title: Defining the User
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that effective websites are designed for people, not just businesses. Define target audience as the primary group of users. Introduce Personas as fictional characters created to represent different user types. Model the difference between demographics and psychographics using Keppel Bay Marina as an example.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the terminology table by matching the definitions and providing an example for each term based on our local marina.

activities.questioning:
Why is 'Age' considered demographic while 'Loves fishing' is psychographic? Expected: Age is a statistical fact about a population, while fishing is an interest or lifestyle trait.
How does knowing someone is a 'Tourist' change what they look for compared to a 'Local Boat Owner'? Expected: Tourists need maps and charter info; owners need fuel prices and berth bookings.
activities.scaffolding: Target Audience: The specific group of people a product is aimed at. Persona: A fictional character that represents a user type. Demographics: Statistical data relating to the population (age, gender, location). Psychographics: The study of people according to their attitudes and aspirations.
activities.eLearning: Monitor students from the rear of the room to ensure they are focusing on the definitions rather than just browsing the marina website.

activities.title: The User Story Framework

Why is the 'so that' part the most important for a designer? Expected: It explains the purpose/value, which helps the designer decide how prominent the feature should be.
activities.scaffolding: Role: Who is using it. Action: What they do. Benefit: Why they do it.
activities.transition: Now that we can identify the parts, let's build some together.

activities.title: Establishing Design Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that design criteria are the 'rules' or 'goals' we use to judge if a design is successful. Differentiate between functional (what it does) and non-functional (how it looks/performs). Use Keppel Bay Marina's mobile responsiveness as a key example of criteria.

activities.questioning:
Why is 'Mobile responsiveness' non-functional? Expected: It's about 'how' the site behaves across devices, not a specific task like 'booking a room'.
What is an example of a functional requirement for a café? Expected: A digital menu or an online booking form.
activities.scaffolding: Functional: Features, tasks, tools (e.g., Search bar). Non-Functional: Quality, speed, appearance, accessibility (e.g., High contrast text).
activities.transition: Once we have our criteria, we can start the fun part: brainstorming.

rows.value: Allow users to book a table online

activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing words to complete your notes on testable design goals.
activities.questioning:

activities.scaffolding: Word Bank: objective, measurable, opinion, testing, accessibility.
activities.transition: With our criteria set, let's generate some creative ideas to meet them.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students move into information architecture, learning how to decompose complex business information into a logical, manageable structure. They explore how to organise content to ensure an efficient user journey, preventing information overload. The primary focus is on planning the navigation flow and visualising the relationship between different pages and sections of the site.

resources.value: Card-sorting kits (physical or digital), diagramming software (e.g., Lucidchart or Draw.io), site map convention guide, examples of poor vs. effective navigation structures.

theory.value: The theory focuses on the principle of decomposition in computational thinking—breaking a website down into its component pages and content blocks. Students learn about different navigational hierarchies, including linear and tree-based structures, and the importance of the 'three-click rule' for user efficiency. Instruction covers the conventions of site mapping, including the use of standardised symbols to represent homepages, parent pages, and external links.

prac.value: Students perform a card-sorting activity to categorise business information (e.g., menus, pricing, contact forms, team bios) into logical groupings. Following this, they use digital diagramming tools to create a comprehensive site map for their chosen local business. This map must show the primary navigation menu and the hierarchy of sub-pages. Students participate in a 'gallery walk' to provide feedback on the logical flow and organisational clarity of each other's proposed site architectures.

assessment.value: Formative: Submission of the digital site map and content decomposition table showing logical grouping of business information.

outlineTheme.value: Students explore information architecture by decomposing the website's content into logical sections and hierarchical structures. They create site maps to plan the navigation flow and determine the most effective way to organise information for their chosen local business. This involves identifying essential pages and ensuring the user journey is efficient and logical.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: The teaching arc moves to visual communication and accessibility, where students explore the impact of colour theory, typography, and layout on user experience. They develop a visual style guide that ensures brand consistency while meeting the diverse accessibility needs of the community. Students investigate how specific design choices, such as high-contrast palettes and readable font pairings, can improve the inclusivity of a digital solution for the Yeppoon community.

resources.value: Adobe Express or Canva, WebAIM Contrast Checker, Google Fonts, WCAG 2.2 'At a Glance' guide, visual style guide templates.

theory.value: Students examine the core principles of visual hierarchy and the psychological impact of colour in branding, specifically focusing on how local businesses use visual cues to signal trust and industry (e.g., coastal blues for tourism or earthy tones for local trades). Explicit instruction is provided on the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), focusing on perceivable and understandable content. Students learn about the importance of sans-serif typography for digital legibility and the technical requirements for colour contrast ratios to support users with visual impairments.

prac.value: Students use digital design tools to create a formal visual style guide for their chosen business. This includes selecting a primary and secondary colour palette using hex codes, defining heading and body font families, and designing standardised button styles. They apply these styles to a mock-up of a 'Hero' section, ensuring the layout follows the F-pattern for readability. Students must use an online contrast checker to validate that their chosen colour combinations meet accessibility standards before finalising their guide.

assessment.value: Formative: Completion of the Visual Style Guide and a short written justification explaining how the design choices support accessibility and business branding.

outlineTheme.value: The teaching arc moves to visual communication and accessibility, where students explore the impact of colour theory, typography, and layout on user experience. They develop a visual style guide that ensures brand consistency while meeting the diverse accessibility needs of the community. Students investigate how specific design choices can improve the inclusivity of a digital solution.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Using divergent design thinking techniques, students generate multiple alternative design ideas and translate their best concepts into detailed wireframes. These low-fidelity prototypes allow students to experiment with page layouts and user interface elements without the constraints of code. They review these wireframes against their initial design criteria to ensure alignment with user stories, focusing on the efficient placement of information such as service lists and contact forms.

resources.value: Figma or Balsamiq, paper-based wireframe templates, sketching timers, examples of common UI design patterns.

theory.value: The theory focuses on the distinction between low-fidelity and high-fidelity prototyping in the design process. Students learn about User Interface (UI) patterns, such as navigation bars, grids, and cards, and how these structures support the user journey planned in Week 3. Instruction covers the use of annotations in wireframes to communicate functionality and responsive design principles, explaining how layouts must adapt from desktop monitors to mobile devices to meet the needs of customers on the move.

prac.value: Students participate in a rapid sketching session, generating three distinct layout variations for their homepage within set time limits. They then transition to a digital wireframing tool to create detailed structural blueprints for three essential pages: Home, Services/Products, and Contact. Students annotate their wireframes to show where specific user stories (e.g., 'As a customer, I want to see a price list') are addressed. Peer feedback is used to evaluate if the layout prioritises the business's 'Call to Action' effectively.

assessment.value: Formative: Submission of three digital wireframes with annotations linked to the design criteria and user stories developed in Week 2.

outlineTheme.value: Using divergent design thinking techniques, students generate multiple alternative design ideas and translate their best concepts into detailed wireframes. These low-fidelity prototypes allow students to experiment with page layouts and user interface elements without the constraints of code. They review these wireframes against their initial design criteria to ensure alignment with user stories.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: In the final implementation phase, students move into structured testing and user trials to validate their digital solution. They engage in peer-testing cycles where they observe other students interacting with their website, looking for navigation bottlenecks or layout breaks. Students collect formal feedback based on their original user stories to determine if the prototype successfully meets the needs of the target audience. The week concludes with a final 'bug-fix' sprint, where students use their collected data to perform iterative improvements to the site's code and usability.

resources.value: Usability testing templates, screen recording tools, project submission portal, final design criteria checklist.

theory.value: The theory focuses on the 'Evaluation' and 'Testing' phases of the design cycle. Students learn about different testing methodologies, such as 'Think Aloud' protocols and usability checklists. Instruction covers how to categorize feedback into 'Critical Bugs' (functionality issues) and 'Enhancements' (aesthetic improvements). Students explore the importance of cross-browser and cross-device testing, understanding why a website might appear differently on a smartphone compared to a desktop monitor. They are also taught how to document these tests as evidence of an iterative design process.

prac.value: Students conduct a formal usability test with two peers, using a structured observation sheet to record how easily the users can find specific information (e.g., 'Find the business phone number' or 'Locate the price list'). They document any identified issues in a simple 'Bug Log'. Following the testing, students return to their code to fix high-priority issues, such as broken links or overlapping text on small screens. The final lessons are dedicated to polishing the code and preparing the design journal for the project submission.

assessment.value: Summative: Final submission of the 'Website Prototype' project, including the functional GitHub site, testing evidence, and the design documentation.

outlineTheme.value: In the testing phase, students conduct structured user trials to collect feedback on the website’s functionality, layout, and usability. They record evidence of bugs or navigation issues and use this data to perform iterative improvements to the prototype. This process ensures the final solution is robust and meets the needs of the identified target audience.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: The final week transitions from development to critical evaluation and professional presentation. Students spend the initial lessons conducting a final quality assurance check on their code to ensure all navigation links and media assets function correctly in the GitHub Codespaces environment. They then shift focus to the formal evaluation of their project, documenting how the final solution aligns with the design criteria and user stories developed at the start of the unit. The unit concludes with a 'Local Business Showcase' where students present their functional prototypes to the class, articulating their design decisions and the role of generative AI in their workflow.

theory.value: Students explore the process of formal product evaluation by comparing the final functional prototype against the design criteria and user stories established in the planning phase. They investigate the concept of 'future-proofing' digital solutions, considering how a local business might scale or update content as their services evolve over time. Explicit instruction is provided on reflective practice, specifically evaluating the impact of generative AI on project efficiency, code accuracy, and the developer's creative process. Students discuss the relationship between meeting initial specifications and achieving high-quality user experiences in a commercial context. They also examine how to articulate the technical strengths and limitations of a digital system when presenting to stakeholders.

prac.value: In the final practical sessions, students apply the results of their Week 9 user trials to execute a 'final polish' of their HTML and CSS files, ensuring cross-device compatibility. They complete their digital design journals by documenting a formal evaluation table that cross-references final website features with the original project requirements. Students prepare a concise visual presentation that demonstrates the navigation flow, accessibility features, and responsiveness of their site to a peer audience. During the class showcase, students use a peer-feedback rubric to evaluate how well their classmates' solutions addressed the specific needs of the chosen Yeppoon business. Finally, they ensure all project files are correctly committed to their GitHub repository for summative assessment submission.

assessment.value: Summative: Final submission of the Website Prototype project (Unit 4 assessment). This includes the functional website repository, the design journal (containing user stories, wireframes, and style guides), and the final written evaluation.

activities.title: Vocabulary of Maintenance
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the concepts of 'future-proofing', 'scalability', and 'technical debt'. Explain that a website is never truly 'finished' as businesses evolve. Provide examples relevant to Yeppoon businesses (e.g., changing seasonal menus or adding new tour dates).

Why is 'Future-proofing' important for a business owner? Expected: It saves money and time by making the site easy to update later.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Future-proofing (designing to minimize future changes), Scalability (the ability to grow), Technical Debt (choosing an easy, messy solution now that causes problems later).
activities.transition: Understanding these terms helps us write professional reflections for the business owner.
activities.workbookMaterials: Vocabulary matching table for digital maintenance terms.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Future-proofing: Designing a site so it doesn't become obsolete quickly. 2. Scalability: The capacity for a system to grow or handle more work. 3. Technical Debt: The implied cost of refactoring messy code chosen for speed.
